clue.text: Grand university institute invested in gold diode that provides illumination in museum

definitions.note: The definition is a relative clause standing in for a noun — the thing that does this — and the illumination it provides is enlightenment rather than light.

parts.note: au is gold's chemical symbol, from the Latin aurum

indicators.note: Money invested in something goes inside it, so the letters named before the phrase are planted within the piece that follows.

parts.note: the clue hands this word over whole, and the insertion splits it after the first three letters
g = grand, as in a thousand pounds
u = university
i = institute

explanation.surface: Serious money poured into a gold diode that lights up a museum.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Illumination' is the trap: it reads as light for the diode and means enlightenment, the kind a recorded commentary gives a visitor. Three one-letter abbreviations queue up before they go in.
explanation.definitionFit: An audio guide talks a visitor through a museum's exhibits, so it lights the place up in the sense of explaining it, not of shining.

clue.text: Likewise, mate's not starting to get round

indicators.note: not starting means the word loses its first letter

parts.note: a mate is a pal, and the possessive gives the S
O is round in shape

explanation.surface: A friend fails to make a start on getting round to something, too.
explanation.walkthrough: 'not starting' takes the P off PALS (mate's), leaving ALS; O for 'round' completes it.
explanation.definitionFit: Also and likewise both mean in addition, in the same way.

clue.text: Feast Ms Blyton knocked up

indicators.note: In a down entry anything knocked up is written from the bottom towards the top, so its letters arrive back to front.

parts.note: Enid Blyton, the children's author of the Famous Five, supplies ENID, and climbing the grid it arrives in this order

explanation.surface: Enid Blyton being roused early for a banquet.
explanation.walkthrough: In Britain 'knocked up' still carries its old sense of being woken by a knock at the door, which is the picture the surface wants. The author's first name is the only material here.
explanation.definitionFit: To dine is to eat a full sit-down meal, and to feast is the same verb with the table more loaded.

clue.text: What poppies do daily is obvious

definitions.note: Poppies open and shut as plain verbs, while the hyphens belong to the adjective of the second definition; one spelling serves both readings.
definitions.meaning: the flowers unfurl in the morning and close again at dusk, every day of their season
said of a case or a question that needs no arguing, settled the moment anyone looks

explanation.surface: A gardener's note on the daily routine of a bed of poppies.
explanation.walkthrough: Poppies unfurl in the morning sun and close again at dusk, day after day. An open-and-shut case is one whose answer is plain the moment anyone looks at it.
explanation.definitionFit: The flowers open and shut each day, quite literally; and a matter that is open-and-shut is obvious, settled at a glance with nothing left to argue.

clue.text: Country, Charles' realm: wet weather on English

indicators.note: In a down clue one thing sits on top of another, so the wet weather goes above the letter named after it.

parts.note: King Charles III reigns over the United Kingdom, and these are its initials
the commonest wet weather there is
e = English

explanation.surface: A forecast for the king's realm: rain moving in over England.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Charles' realm' is the country you are invited to settle for, and it supplies only the first two letters. In a down entry 'on' stacks one piece above the next.
explanation.definitionFit: Ukraine is a sovereign country in eastern Europe, so the first word of the clue names the answer as plainly as a clue ever does.

clue.text: Cavorting, randier, where dishes are seen

definitions.note: The definition is a 'where' phrase rather than a noun: the answer is the place it describes.

indicators.note: Cavorting is leaping about with no order to it, and letters told to cavort will not stay in the sequence they were given.

parts.note: anagram fodder, seven letters

explanation.surface: Frisky company larking about somewhere the dishes are on show.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dishes' keeps the randy surface going — attractive people, not crockery. A drainer is the rack or ridged board beside a British sink where the washing-up is stood to dry.
explanation.definitionFit: Washed plates are stacked on a drainer to drip dry, so it is exactly the spot where dishes are on display.

clue.text: Everyman's adding additional remarks for naughty children

indicators.note: Adding one thing to another puts them end to end, so what comes next is tacked straight on to what came before.

parts.note: Everyman is the setter's own name, so 'Everyman's' is him saying I'M
a PS is the postscript added below a letter's signature

explanation.surface: The setter tacking a few extra remarks on at the end for some badly behaved children.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Everyman' is the Observer setter's pen name, so 'Everyman's' is him saying I'm — a trick this puzzle plays most weeks. The definition waits at the far end, past a link word.
explanation.definitionFit: Imps are small mischievous demons, and the word has long been used half-fondly of children who will not behave.

clue.text: Spoil old lady and sons eating last of quince jams

parts.note: to mar is to spoil
MA is a familiar word for one's mother, one's old lady

indicators.note: eating means the boys take the following letter inside them

parts.note: sons are lads

indicators.note: the last of a word is its final letter

explanation.surface: Indulging an elderly woman and her boys, who are tucking into quince preserves.
explanation.definitionFit: Marmalades are citrus preserves, and the word once covered quince conserve too, so they are kinds of fruit spread.

clue.text: Characteristic of the broth or the stout?

definitions.meaning: read as a bowl of soup, and pointing at the other word for one — broth is stock, and the first half of the grid entry says so
read as a glass of dark Irish beer, and meant as a stout person, someone solidly built

explanation.surface: A menu question about what the soup and the beer have in common.
explanation.walkthrough: Both halves turn on a second sense: stock is the broth itself, and 'stout' described a thickset build long before it named a drink. No word here hands over a letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Stockiness is a short, solid, thickset build, which is what stout means of a person, while broth is stock — so one word answers for both.

clue.text: Maybe nose around, enrage sons?

indicators.note: Something sent around travels in no fixed direction, and the letters beside it come to rest in an order nobody chose.

parts.note: anagram fodder, ten letters

explanation.surface: A parent poking their nose in and infuriating the boys.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Maybe' is the flag that the definition is one example standing for its whole class. An indicator that also fits the surface is the hardest kind to spot: 'nose around' reads as a single phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: The nose is one of the body's sense organs, smell being its sense, and 'maybe' marks it as an example rather than the class itself.

clue.text: Naked war god in Jason's ship

indicators.note: Something naked has had its outer covering taken off, so the first and last letters of the words beside it come away.

parts.note: strip the outside letters from WAR GOD — the w and the d — and what is left runs straight on

explanation.surface: A stripped statue of the war god riding on Jason's ship.
explanation.walkthrough: The war god is a red herring: Ares and Mars both suit the surface and neither supplies a letter, because the phrase is being read as ink on the page. The Argonauts are named after the vessel.
explanation.definitionFit: The Argo is the ship Jason sailed in search of the Golden Fleece, crewed by the heroes who took their name from it.

clue.text: Land with mountain, protected place?

parts.note: a nation is a land in the sense of a whole country
an alp is the crossword's standard mountain, from the range itself
Noah's ark was built to keep its passengers safe from the flood

explanation.walkthrough: Every word works twice: read straight the clue describes the answer, and read as instructions three nouns queue up in order. 'Protected place' is both the ark and the whole point.
explanation.definitionFit: Read straight, the clue says what the answer is: a tract of country, mountains and all, that the state protects from development.

clue.text: Easy Street? Roll eye twice if dubious

indicators.note: dubious means questionable or shady, so these letters are rearranged
twice says the word if is written two times

explanation.surface: Someone rolls their eyes at a doubtful promise of a comfortable life.
explanation.walkthrough: 'twice' gives IFIF; 'dubious' scrambles it with ROLL and EYE.
explanation.definitionFit: Easy Street is an American idiom for a carefree, prosperous existence; this is the British equivalent.

clue.text: Workers make this — for George's birthday party?

definitions.note: The definition names the answer by who produces it rather than by a synonym, and the workers are the bees of a hive, not people.

parts.note: Prince George is a young member of the royal family, so anything of his is a royal one
jelly, the wobbly gelatin dessert Americans call Jell-O, is the fixture of a British children's birthday tea

explanation.surface: Wondering what to lay on for young Prince George's birthday party.
explanation.walkthrough: The workers are bees: the caste that feeds this to the larvae chosen to become queens. The dash does the work of a colon, definition on one side and party on the other.
explanation.definitionFit: Royal jelly is the protein-rich secretion worker bees produce and feed to a chosen larva so that it grows into a queen, so the workers really do make it.

clue.text: Tudor monarch and his antagonist welcoming love for sculptor

parts.note: Henry VIII is the Tudor king every clue means

indicators.note: A host welcoming a guest takes them inside, so the letter that follows goes within the piece before it.

parts.note: Sir Thomas More refused to accept that king as head of the church, and lost his head over it
love is the tennis score of nothing, written as this letter

explanation.surface: The Tudor king and the man who defied him embracing, with affection winning out.
explanation.walkthrough: Two men from the 1530s stack up into a twentieth-century name. Henry Moore was the Yorkshire miner's son whose holed bronze reclining figures sit in parks and galleries around the world.
explanation.definitionFit: Henry Moore is the British sculptor of those big reclining bronzes, the best-known English sculptor of the last century.

clue.text: Outstanding, like an Italian three-year-old?

parts.note: a child of three has gone past the age of two, which is to say over it
due is the Italian for two, the number the child is past

explanation.surface: An Italian toddler who has just had a third birthday.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Outstanding' is the trap — not excellent but unpaid, the sense a bill has. Italian numbers earn their keep in crosswords for their spellings, and due is two.
explanation.definitionFit: A bill still outstanding is one that has gone unpaid past its date, which is exactly what calling it overdue says.

clue.text: Match official with reason to stop play that's often repeated

definitions.note: The definition is a relative clause — the thing that is often repeated — standing in for the noun the answer is.

parts.note: the ref is the referee running a match
'rain stopped play' is the standing announcement at a British cricket match when the weather closes in

explanation.surface: A referee and the weather between them bringing a match to a halt.
explanation.walkthrough: Cricket in Britain is abandoned for weather often enough that 'rain stopped play' became a phrase in its own right. A refrain is the chorus a song brings back after every verse.
explanation.definitionFit: A refrain is the line or chorus that returns at the end of each verse, so being repeated is the whole of what makes it one.

clue.text: Publicises trendy zeppelin

parts.note: to air a grievance is to publicise it
hip = trendy

explanation.surface: A headline about a fashionable balloon being advertised.
explanation.walkthrough: Zeppelin was a German count whose rigid craft bombed London in the first world war, and his name stuck to the type. The join between the two pieces hides inside the s.
explanation.definitionFit: A zeppelin is the rigid German make of airship, famous enough that its name came to stand for the whole class of them.

clue.text: At the outset, partially render edible (cleverly orchestrating orderly kitchen?)

definitions.text: At the outset, partially render edible

indicators.note: At the outset means right at the start, so only the opening letter of each word that follows is wanted.

parts.words: partially render edible (cleverly orchestrating orderly kitchen
parts.note: the initial letters of those seven words, taken in order

explanation.surface: A boast about a cleverly organised, orderly kitchen.
explanation.walkthrough: The bracketed praise for the kitchen exists to supply four more initials while keeping the line sounding like a chef's note. Read straight, the whole sentence says what the answer means.
explanation.definitionFit: To precook is exactly this: at the outset, and only partly, to make food edible before the real cooking begins.

clue.text: A skyscraper has many tales to be told

definitions.note: The definition is a sentence with the answer as its missing object — a skyscraper has many of them — rather than a noun phrase.

indicators.note: A tale is told aloud, so the word is to be heard rather than read, and what reaches the grid need only sound the same.

parts.note: tales are stories, and British English spells the floors of a building the other way

explanation.surface: A tall building with plenty of tales attached to it.
explanation.walkthrough: British English keeps two spellings for the one sound — stories are the tales, storeys the floors — while American English uses 'stories' for both. The definition is the first four words, dressed up as scene-setting.
explanation.definitionFit: A skyscraper is tall because it stacks storeys, one floor above another, by the dozen.

clue.text: 'Not available'? Artist has risen, extremely heated

indicators.note: In a down clue whatever has risen has travelled upwards, so those letters are written back to front.

parts.note: na is what a form says against something not available
an RA is a Royal Academician, the crossword's standard artist
the clue's own word, taken as it stands

explanation.surface: An artist marked down as unavailable has got up in a temper.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Heated' pulls towards temper and delivers a climate instead. Everything before the comma is read from the bottom of the entry upwards, which is what 'risen' asks of a down clue.
explanation.definitionFit: The Sahara is the vast desert across northern Africa, and Saharan is used of anything as blisteringly hot as it is.

clue.text: Hong Kong hamper just about to go stale

indicators.note: Letters thrown about land where they will, in an order nobody arranged.

parts.note: hk = Hong Kong, the territory's standard short form, joining the fodder
anagram fodder, ten letters

explanation.surface: A gift basket from Hong Kong that is nearly past its best.
explanation.walkthrough: The phrase comes from an episode of Happy Days in which Fonzie waterskied over a shark — the moment fans point to as the series losing it. 'Hamper' is a basket here, not a verb.
explanation.definitionFit: A show that has jumped the shark has passed its peak and gone stale, reaching for stunts because the good ideas have run out.

clue.text: Ornamental case kept in perpetuity

indicators.note: What is kept in something lies inside it, so the letters sit unbroken within the word that follows.

parts.note: these four letters sit in order across the middle of the long word

explanation.surface: Something decorative held on to for ever.
explanation.walkthrough: An etui is a small ornamental case for needles, scissors or a thimble, a French word that survives in English mainly through crosswords and its handy vowels.
explanation.definitionFit: An etui is a little decorated box or sheath for sewing tools, made to be looked at as well as used.

clue.text: Snakes in midsts of grassy copses

indicators.note: the midst of something is its centre, so take the middle two letters of each word

explanation.surface: Snakes lurk in the middle of grassy copses.
explanation.definitionFit: Asps are small venomous snakes, such as the one that killed Cleopatra.

clue.text: Money, convenience, time

parts.note: a public convenience is a lavatory, and the loo is what Britain calls it
t = time

explanation.surface: Three things a shopper weighs up: the cost, the handiness, the wait.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Convenience' is the British public lavatory, a sense that survives on street signs, and the commas are doing the work of plus signs. Loot is money as plunder rather than wages.
explanation.definitionFit: Loot is money with the taint on it — the haul from a robbery or a raid — but money all the same.

clue.text: Old seaport resort: they'll tell you who lives here

definitions.text: they'll tell you who lives here
definitions.note: The definition is a whole clause about what the things do rather than a noun, and 'here' is the house whose door they are screwed to.

indicators.note: To re-sort is to sort again, putting the letters into a fresh arrangement; the seaside sense belongs to the surface only.

parts.note: anagram fodder, ten letters

explanation.surface: An old seaside town where you can find out who lives where.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Resort' completes the holiday picture and carries the instruction: re-sort. Door-plates are the engraved name plates beside a front door or a doctor's entrance.
explanation.definitionFit: A door-plate carries the occupant's name at the entrance, which is how it announces to a caller who lives inside.

clue.text: Frenchman: Adam's partner, you say?

definitions.note: The answer is a French forename rather than a word meaning Frenchman: the definition points at the sort of man who is called it.

indicators.note: 'You say' asks for the sound of the words rather than their spelling, so what goes in the grid need only be heard the same.

parts.note: Adam's partner in Genesis is Eve, and her name with the possessive is said much as the French name is

explanation.surface: A Frenchman identified as Adam's other half.
explanation.walkthrough: The apostrophe-s is part of the sound rather than a possessive to be undone, which is the whole step here. Yves Saint Laurent is where most readers will have met the name.
explanation.definitionFit: Yves is a common French man's forename — Saint Laurent, Klein, Montand — so a man answering to it is a Frenchman.

clue.text: Barely crawls?

definitions.meaning: read as scarcely, and meant as bare — with nothing on
read as inching along, and meant as swimming, since the crawl is a stroke

explanation.surface: Something moving so slowly it is scarcely getting along at all.
explanation.walkthrough: The crawl is a swimming stroke, so 'crawls' is swims, and 'barely' is bare rather than scarcely. Skinny-dipping is swimming with no costume on, traditionally after dark.
explanation.definitionFit: To skinny-dip is to swim with nothing on — bare — so both words of the clue arrive at the answer once each is read the other way.
